newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine farm growth brightens economic outlook.
newsitem.headline: Philippine farm growth brightens economic outlook.

text.p: Robust agricultural growth in the first quarter has fuelled hopes the Philippine economy will remain healthy despite gloom on the stock market, analysts said on Wednesday.
The agriculture sector grew 4.22 percent in the first three months, up from 2.49 percent in the year-earlier quarter, according to the Bureau of Agricultural Statistics.

That growth is even more impressive when compared to adjusted figures issued by another government office, the National Economic Development Authority, which said the sector had actually contracted 3.04 percent in the first quarter of 1996.
The figures boosted the Manila stock market, which had sunk to 17-month lows on fears that problems in Thailand's banking and property sectors would be repeated in the Philippines.
On Wednesday, the market index gained 1.58 percent to 2,547.36 points.

"Part of the confidence is brought about by the agricultural growth figure for the first quarter, a good indication that maybe the GNP (gross national product) figure is within target," said Asiamerit Securities analyst Ramon Saulo.
The government is scheduled to release first quarter economic growth figures next week.
Government estimates put GNP growth at seven to eight percent this year versus 6.8 percent last year. Gross domestic product growth is projected at over six percent compared with 5.5 percent.

The growth in the farm sector, which accounts for 21 percent of economic output, compared to 24 percent for manufacturing and is the latest data attesting to the soundness of the country's economy, economists said.
Last week, the government reported growth in the first quarter trade deficit slowed to 8.4 percent versus 41 percent growth a year ago.
"The numbers are good," said Conrad Andres, research head of DBP-Daiwa Securities. "That should offset the slowdown in manufacturing."
The index of manufacturing production volume fell 1.8 percent year-on-year in the first two months, largely due to declines in garments, transport equipment and paper products.
Andres said he expected gross domestic product in the first quarter to be above five percent.

"(But) the stock market would like to see the total picture. There is still some concern manufacturing didn't do as well...which was fed by the poor corporate results," said Luz Lorenzo, economist at Peregrine Securities.
"I still think GNP will still be all right," said Omar Cruz, vice president of Citibank. "Nothing has happened which should affect GNP even if corporate earnings are suffering."
Cruz said blue chip companies such as food and beverage giant San Miguel Corp reported dismal earnings because of stiffer competition from imports.
"The purchasing power is still there. It just shifted to more competitive imported products," Cruz argued. "On aggregate, the pie has continued to increase."
"That is the effect of industrial restructuring... the effect of liberalisation," which should eventually force local companies to be more efficient, he said.
